content.title: About
content.content: Bagel with oat bran is a whole‑grain baked product that incorporates oat bran into the dough. It features a crisp crust, a slightly dense crumb, and a subtle nutty aroma from the bran.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat bran is rich in beta‑glucan, which helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels.
Traditional bagels are boiled before baking, giving them their characteristic chewy texture.
Oat bran is a by‑product of oat processing and is often used to boost the nutritional profile of foods.
Bagels are commonly served with seeds, cheese, or vegetables, but they are also tasty plain.
In recent years, oat‑bran bagels have gained popularity among health‑conscious consumers.

items.title: High in beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan can lower LDL cholesterol and supports immune function.

items.title: Rich source of dietary fiber
items.content: Oat bran adds both soluble and insoluble fiber, improving digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for energy metabolism, muscle function, and nerve health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Bagel with oat bran raises blood sugar more slowly than typical white bakery products.

items.title: B vitamins
items.content: Oat bran provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system support.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to oats or oat bran, experiencing skin rashes, itching, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on equipment shared with wheat, so the product may contain trace gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite its fiber content, the bagel is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is important for weight management.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or heat treatment lowers its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bagel with oat bran can be enjoyed as a snack, sliced and topped with cream cheese, avocado, or hummus, added to sandwiches, salads, or soups. Toasting it adds a pleasant crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bagels in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent drying out and mold growth. Discard any bagels that develop a stale or off odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn Puffs are light, airy snacks made from whole corn that is steamed and extruded at high temperature. They have a crunchy texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and are often enjoyed as part of breakfast or as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn puffs first appeared in the United States in the 1950s as an alternative to traditional wheat cereals.
Extrusion preserves most of corn's nutrients, including fiber and B‑vitamins.
The puffs are often lightly coated with sugar or salt to enhance taste.
The corn used is frequently grown without genetically modified seeds in organic lines.
In some countries they are used in children’s meals because of their soft texture and easy digestibility.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn puffs provide steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, corn puffs contain almost no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Gluten‑free (when made from gluten‑free corn)
items.content: Gluten‑free versions are available for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Some varieties can raise blood sugar quickly due to rapid digestion.

items.title: Added sugar or salt
items.content: Certain products contain added sugar or salt, which may be undesirable for specific dietary plans.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: As with any grain product, puffs may contain trace pesticide residues if not grown organically.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn puffs can be eaten dry as a snack, added to milk, yogurt or kefir, used in dessert recipes, granola mixes, or as a coating for fish and chicken.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store puffs in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, transfer to an airtight container to keep them crunchy.

chicken-breast-fried-coated-skin-coating.title: Chicken breast, fried, coated, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast, fried in a coating, is made from pre‑cooked meat (code 776). The skin is not consumed. The product has a crispy golden crust and a tender interior that is rich in protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The coating usually consists of flour, spices and sometimes breadcrumbs.
High‑temperature frying preserves most of the protein but adds calories from fat.
Chicken breast is one of the leanest cuts of poultry, but the coating raises its energy value.
This type of product is traditionally served in fast‑food outlets, cafeterias and ready‑meal dishes.
Code 776 in the database indicates pre‑cooked meat that is then fried.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content in raw form
items.content: When boiled, the breast contains almost no fat; most of the fat comes from the frying step.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune function.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Chicken meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The coating often contains salt; people monitoring sodium intake should take this into account.

items.title: Trans fats in frying oil
items.content: Using oils high in trans fats can make the product less healthy.

items.title: Contamination if stored improperly
items.content: If kept above 4 °C for more than 2 days, bacterial growth risk increases.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat hot. It can be served with vegetable sides, sauces, in salads, or used in sandwiches. Remove the skin before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at +2…+4 °C in the original packaging for up to 3 days. For longer storage freeze at –18 °C, where the shelf life extends to 2 months. Before eating, check that there is no off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled eggs are hard‑boiled chicken eggs that have been peeled and soaked in a brine made with vinegar, spices, and sometimes vegetables. They have a firm texture, a mildly sour taste, and a distinctive spice aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled eggs are a traditional snack in Eastern Europe and Russia, especially during holidays.
Typical brine ingredients include vinegar, salt, sugar, mustard, pepper, bay leaf, and coriander.
When fully submerged in brine, they can be kept in the refrigerator for 2–3 weeks.
In some regions beetroot is added to the brine, giving the eggs a bright red color.
Pickled eggs are often served as a bar snack with beer or as part of salads.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs provide complete protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D helps maintain bone health and supports immune function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Eggs supply selenium, phosphorus, and iron, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Probiotic effect
items.content: Fermentation in the brine can promote beneficial bacteria, aiding gut microbiota balance.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins, ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled eggs are salty; people with hypertension should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If the brine is not acidic enough or eggs are stored at improper temperatures, harmful bacteria can grow.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; those with elevated cholesterol levels should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled eggs can be eaten straight as a snack, sliced into salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a garnish for canapés. They are usually served cold, sometimes with mustard or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pickled eggs in the refrigerator in a sealed container, fully covered by brine. At 0‑4 °C they stay good for 2–3 weeks. Discard any eggs if the brine becomes cloudy, develops an off‑odor, or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy green vegetable that originated in Central and Southwest Asia. Its tender, dark green leaves have a mild, slightly earthy flavor. Spinach is eaten raw in salads and smoothies or cooked in soups, pies, pastas, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is thought to have originated in ancient Persia and spread to Europe in the Middle Ages.
Spinach leaves shrink dramatically when cooked, so a large bag of leaves yields only a small amount.
Baby spinach is harvested young and has smaller, more tender leaves.
Spinach contains naturally occurring nitrates, which are also found in other leafy vegetables.
Spinach is a member of the amaranth family, related to beets and quinoa.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Spinach is an excellent source of vitamin K, which supports normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides vitamin A and vitamin C
items.content: Spinach contains carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A, as well as vitamin C.

items.title: Contains folate and minerals
items.content: Spinach provides folate, iron, magnesium, and potassium.

items.title: Contains eye-supporting carotenoids
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin are plant pigments associated with eye health.

items.title: Very low in calories
items.content: Spinach is low in calories and adds nutrients and volume to meals.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach is high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people and may reduce the absorption of calcium and iron.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Spinach contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Raw leafy greens can carry bacteria, so wash them well and avoid leaves that are slimy or spoiled.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Spinach allergy is uncommon but can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spinach can be eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, and smoothies or cooked by sautéing, steaming, or adding it to soups, omelets, pasta, and pies. It wilts within minutes of heating, so add it near the end of cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unwashed spinach in the refrigerator in a container or bag with a paper towel to absorb moisture, where it usually keeps for three to five days. Wash it right before use. Spinach can also be blanched and frozen.
